entities.summary:
Anthropology is the scientific and humanistic study of humanity in its full biological, social, cultural, and linguistic diversity — across all times and places. As the broadest of the human sciences, anthropology encompasses four major subfields: biological/physical anthropology (human evolution and variation), cultural/social anthropology (social organization, belief systems, kinship, and meaning), linguistic anthropology (the relationship between language and culture), and archaeology (the study of the human past through material remains).

The discipline emerged formally in the 19th century from the collision of evolutionary theory, colonial encounter, and comparative philology. E.B. Tylor's Primitive Culture (1871) coined the first systematic definition of culture; Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society (1877) proposed evolutionary stages of social development that influenced Marx and Engels. Franz Boas, working at Columbia University from the 1890s, fundamentally redirected American anthropology by debunking scientific racism and establishing cultural relativism — the principle that cultures must be understood on their own terms, not ranked on an evolutionary scale. Bronisław Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) established long-term participant observation (fieldwork) as the discipline's core method.

20th-century anthropology diversified into structural anthropology (Lévi-Strauss), interpretive anthropology (Clifford Geertz), feminist anthropology, and post-colonial critique. Anthropology's findings — that race is a social construct, that cultural variation is not hierarchical, that every human society has complex systems of meaning — have been among the most politically significant contributions of any academic discipline to modern thought.
